blocks.text: The second is that of Jonathan and of the Jerusalem Targumist, of whom one has here מינקת חויא, and the other פלית חויא, or פיילת חויא. So it should be read, not חיוא as in the Lexicon Baal-Aruch. The lexicographers understand neither. For it is [II, 488] beside the point that they take פליית here for a locust, as in פליא ביארי in chapter 9 of the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath. For פליא ביארי is one thing, פליית חויא another. Namely, the very thing that the Arabs call فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī] phaliath alaphai, that is, the searcher of serpents, or of vipers (as they have taught us above ^{b)} is the name of a spotted kind of beetle which usually lives with scorpions and serpents in the lair of the land crocodile), that very thing, I say, is the Chaldee פליית חויא. For to them חויא is serpent, and פליית paljath, or phaljath, is plainly derived from the Arabic فالية [fāliya] phaliath, which we render searcher, because فلي [falā] phala means to search. Thus فلي الراس [falā al-raʾs] he searched the head, in order to look for lice in it; [col. 1065] فلي الشعر [falā al-shiʿr] he searched the poem, that is, he explored and examined it so as to penetrate the poet's mind. And this kind of beetle is rightly said to search serpents, since it lives continually with them in the same lair, and so constantly accompanies the serpents, whether coming or going, so that by its arrival or its departure it signals that they are near or absent. Hence the proverb current among the Arabs, اتكلم فالية الافاعي [a-takallama fāliyat al-afāʿī] Have you spoken with phaliath alaphai, the searcher of serpents? This is used لاول شر ينتظر بعده شر منه [li-awwal sharr yuntaẓar baʿdahu sharr minhu] of a first evil after which another is expected to arise from it. But since the verb فلي [falā] phala means not only to search but also to nourish and to rear, Jonathan, instead of פליית חויא, has מינקת חויא, i.e. nurse of the serpent. Further, why the two Chaldee translators wished this kind of beetle to be denoted by the word אנקה anaka, I see no reason except the very order of the words. Namely, as the word צב tsab signifies the land crocodile, as we have proved at length ^{c)}, so the following אנקה anaka seemed to signify פליית חויא, that is, the searcher of the serpent, which is the constant attendant of the land crocodile and usually lives in the same lair with it. But this reason, such as it is, carries little weight with me, as does the version itself, which seems to rest on it. Something I had nearly omitted: to some of the Arabs these little creatures are not beetles but بنات وردان [banāt wardān] benath vvardan, the name by which Abenbitar calls the σίλφας [silphas] of Dioscorides, or blattae [cockroaches].

In the third place I count those for whom אנקה anaka is a kind of lizard, who are neither few nor to be despised. For in the Syriac we find ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, which the most learned of the Maronites, the late Gabriel Sionita (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), explained as lizard. In the Samaritan [?] semamitha, that is, stellio, as will become clear in its place. In Erpenius' Arabic الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, that is, a species of lizard which the barbarians call guaril. In the Arabic edited at Paris, الورك [al-wark] alvvarco, which is the same.
